groups.title: Core Ruby Language Concepts
groups.question: You are writing a small Ruby script that groups a list of orders by status, totals them and handles a missing file. Explain the Ruby features you would use.

followUps.Variables, methods, and blocks in Ruby: What is a block in Ruby and how do methods use it?
followUps.Arrays, hashes, and Enumerable module: How would you use Enumerable to filter and total orders?
followUps.Symbols, ranges, and exception handling: Why are symbols used as hash keys, and how does Ruby handle exceptions?

evidence.text: Ruby variables have no declared types; values carry their own type.
A block is a chunk of code passed to a method with do...end or braces.
Blocks can use variables from the surrounding scope, and methods run them with yield or by iterating.
Arrays and hashes are objects with rich methods.
Enumerable provides methods like map, select and reduce for iterating.
These replace manual loops with clear, chainable expressions.
Symbols are immutable names that are reused rather than recreated, which suits hash keys.
Ranges represent sequences such as 1 to 10.
begin, rescue and ensure catch errors and run cleanup code.

groups.title: Object-Oriented Ruby
groups.question: Two unrelated classes in your app need the same logging behaviour, and the app depends on several libraries. Explain how Ruby shares behaviour and manages dependencies.

followUps.Classes, modules, and mixins pattern: How do modules let unrelated classes share methods?
followUps.Gems and Bundler dependency management: What do the Gemfile and Gemfile.lock do?

evidence.text: A Ruby class can inherit from only one parent class.
Modules can be included in any class to add shared methods.
This shares behaviour without forcing an inheritance relationship.
Gems are Ruby libraries.
The Gemfile lists the gems a project needs.
Bundler records exact versions in the lockfile so every machine uses the same ones.

groups.title: Ruby Tooling and Environment
groups.question: You maintain two apps that need different Ruby versions, and you want to try out code quickly. Explain the tools you would use.

followUps.Installing Ruby with rbenv or RVM: Why use a version manager like rbenv?

evidence.text: Version managers install several Ruby versions side by side.
Each project can use its own version.
This prevents one app's upgrade from breaking another.
IRB is Ruby's interactive shell.
You can try expressions and methods instantly.
It helps check how code behaves before writing it into files.

groups.title: Practical Ruby Patterns
groups.question: Code reviews keep arguing about style and a bug only shows up deep in a method. Explain how you would keep code idiomatic and debug it.

followUps.Writing idiomatic Ruby with style guides: What does RuboCop do for a team?
followUps.Debugging Ruby code with Pry and byebug: How do Pry and byebug help debug Ruby?

evidence.text: RuboCop checks code against a community style guide.
It encourages idioms like guard clauses and clear method names.
Automated checks keep style consistent and end style debates in review.

notEnough: Only saying it is a linter.

evidence.text: They pause execution at a point you choose.
You can inspect variables and objects at that point.
byebug lets you step through code line by line.
